title: 0. Profile, budget, evidence tiers
md:
Two languages from zero to B1 by 31 Dec 2027 on ~14 h/week is feasible for German and marginal for Hungarian; the plan below only works if the hours are structured, not browsed. From 26 Oct 2026 to 31 Dec 2027 is 61 weeks. At 90–120 min on weekdays and 3 h+ on weekend days you have 13–15 h/week, about 850 h total, split 50/50: ~425 h per language. Goethe's own planning figure for B1 is 350–650 lesson hours; German at 425 structured hours is inside that. FSI's 1,100 class hours take Hungarian to ILR 3; B1 (ILR 1+) sits roughly 40% of the way in, so ~450 h with no instructor is the thin end. Treat Hungarian B1 as the target and A2+ as the floor that still serves the consulate interview.

| Field | Value used in this doctrine |
| --- | --- |
| Native language | American English only |
| German | Zero → CEFR B1 (ILR 1+/2) by end of 2027, Goethe-Zertifikat B1 or telc B1 as the external check. Purpose: Ausbildung workplace, German bureaucracy, later Switzerland. Hochdeutsch first; Swiss German listening from month 10. |
| Hungarian | Zero → B1 by end of 2027. Purpose: in-person consulate interview for simplified naturalisation (reported bar: hold an everyday conversation about yourself and your family unaided). |
| Priority | Equal weight, 50/50, run as a staggered start (see C). |
| Time | 90–120 min weekdays, 3 h+ weekend days; ~14 h/week. |
| Setting | Fully self-directed; no classroom; no coding. |
| Equipment | PC + browser, phone, headphones, mic. |

Assumptions added: (1) weekday sessions start after the work shift ends, so the two languages get different clock slots; (2) weekend days hold two sessions, one per language; (3) one paid 30-minute tutor session per language per week is affordable (≈ $8–15 each on marketplace rates); (4) the Hungarian interview rewards spoken biography and family vocabulary more than writing, so Hungarian writing stays minimal.

**Evidence tiers used throughout.** [DOCUMENTED] = public curricula and standards: FSI Basic Course drill design (the public-domain FSI German Basic Course and FSI Hungarian Basic Course), DLI listening/transcription practice as described in its public course materials and the ILR skill-level descriptors, DLPT structure, Goethe/telc B1 specifications. [REPORTED] = credibly described in declassified files, memoirs and serious journalism: KGB Directorate S illegals' legend-building, in-country immersion, and rehearsed interrogation (e.g. the Mitrokhin material, memoirs of former illegals, reporting on the 2010 US arrests). [RECONSTRUCTED] = my synthesis. Where the intelligence label is branding on a mainstream technique, the mainstream origin is named: shadowing comes from interpreter training and Alexander Arguelles; sensory encoding from Stanislavski's method and keyword mnemonics; drills from Fries/Lado audio-lingualism that FSI adopted.

**How to read.** Every technique ends in a numbered protocol: material, minutes, scoring, pass line. P-numbers are referenced by the daily plan (D1) and by the app (Part 2).

# Part 1 — Declassified Linguistic Doctrine

title: A1. FSI/CIA audio-lingual drilling [DOCUMENTED]
md:
**Mechanism.** A drill removes the choice of what to say so that all attention goes to how it is said. The cue (a model sentence plus one changed element) fixes the content; the learner produces the whole sentence within 2–4 seconds. Repeated under time pressure, the case ending, verb slot or suffix stops being computed and becomes a motor-speech habit — the same proceduralisation that lets a native pick *dem* over *den* without knowing the rule. The FSI Basic Courses are built on this: each unit is basic sentences → pronunciation → pattern drills → conversation practice. The tapes run at native tempo with a fixed pause for the response, then the correct form, then a repeat. The CIA's language school used the same audio-lingual design (public FSI materials and Fries/Lado structural linguistics; nothing beyond that is documented, so no claim about CIA-specific drill types is made).

**Drill types, with one worked chain each.**

| Type | What changes | German chain | Hungarian chain |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Substitution | One slot swapped; everything else re-agrees | Ich sehe den Mann. (die Frau) → Ich sehe die Frau. (das Kind) → Ich sehe das Kind. (der Chef) → Ich sehe den Chef. | A boltban vagyok. (az iskola) → Az iskolában vagyok. (a kert) → A kertben vagyok. (a könyvtár) → A könyvtárban vagyok. |
| Transformation: statement ↔ question | Verb to first position / intonation | Er arbeitet heute. → Arbeitet er heute? | Ez a ház nagy. → Nagy ez a ház? |
| Transformation: present → past | Perfekt bracket / past suffix | Ich arbeite in der Werkstatt. → Ich habe in der Werkstatt gearbeitet. | Budapesten dolgozom. → Budapesten dolgoztam. |
| Transformation: affirmative → negative | nicht/kein placement; nem + coverb split | Ich habe Zeit. → Ich habe keine Zeit. / Er kommt heute. → Er kommt heute nicht. | Megírom a levelet. → Nem írom meg a levelet. |
| Transformation: main → subordinate | Verb to clause end (DE); conjunction only (HU) | Ich komme nicht. Ich bin krank. (weil) → Ich komme nicht, weil ich krank bin. | Tudom. Péter beteg. (hogy) → Tudom, hogy Péter beteg. |
| Transformation: indefinite → definite (HU only) | Conjugation switches with the object | — | Olvasok egy könyvet. → Olvasom a könyvet. |
| Expansion | Add a cued element in its correct slot | Ich fahre. (morgen) → Ich fahre morgen. (mit dem Zug) → Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug. (nach Berlin) → Ich fahre morgen mit dem Zug nach Berlin. | Megyek. (a boltba) → Megyek a boltba. (holnap) → Holnap megyek a boltba. |
| Response | Natural short answer to a question | Wann fängt die Schicht an? → Die Schicht fängt um sechs an. | Hol dolgozol? → Egy gyárban dolgozom. |

**Cadence and speed targets.** Cue at native tempo → response window → model answer → learner repeats the model once. Windows: 4 s for one-feature items (a single case ending, one suffix), 6 s for two-feature items (case + adjective ending; possessive + case), 8 s for clause transformations. A response that starts after the window counts as a miss even if correct: the point is reflex, and a slow correct answer is a translated answer. Thirty to forty cues per drill block; never more than ten in a row from one family (interleaving, below).

**Known failure mode and the FSI fix.** Audio-lingualism's documented failure is mechanical fluency: the learner can run the pattern but cannot use it when the content is real, because the drill never asked what the sentence meant. FSI's structural answer is the unit shape itself — drills feed directly into "conversation practice" built from the same sentences, the same day. Keep that coupling absolute: every drill block ends with a 3-minute bridge in which three of the drilled sentences are used for real (ordering, asking a landlord, answering a consular officer).

**Mainstream corrections integrated [RECONSTRUCTED from research].** (1) Interleave families within a block (mix dative, two-way prepositions and separable verbs) rather than drilling one family for twenty minutes: blocked practice gives fast in-session gains and poor retention; interleaved practice does the reverse, which is what you want. (2) Schedule drill items with FSRS-style spaced repetition rather than FSI's fixed re-entry schedule; the app does this. (3) Drills do not supply vocabulary breadth or listening tolerance; comprehensible input (A2) does. Drills build accuracy and speed on top of input, not instead of it.

**Protocol P-1 — Reflex drill block.**

1. Material: app Drill Engine (Part 2, Module 1), or the FSI Basic Course drill tapes for the current unit.
2. Duration: 15 min per language per day (20 min in the 150-min plan). 30–40 cues, interleaved across ≥ 3 families.
3. Procedure: hear/see cue → say the full sentence aloud within the window → reveal → repeat the model once aloud → self-grade (1 = correct and in time, 2 = correct but late or self-corrected, 3 = wrong).
4. Scoring: block score = correct-in-time ÷ cues. Log every 3 and every repeated 2 to the burn book (D9).
5. Pass: ≥ 90% correct and ≥ 80% in time across two consecutive blocks on a set → the set moves to maintenance (SRS only). Below 70% → halve the set and add the family's explanation drill (deconstructor) before the next block.
6. Bridge: 3 min, use three drilled sentences in a spoken mini-scene. Not optional.

title: A2. DLI/FBI operational immersion and gisting
md:
**What is documented.** [DOCUMENTED] DLI's basic courses front-load listening on authentic audio from early in the course and test it on the DLPT (listening and reading, multiple-choice, scored on the ILR scale); speaking is tested by the OPI. Cryptologic and FBI linguists are hired and rated on ILR listening/reading/speaking levels and spend most of their working hours monitoring, gisting (summarising the operationally relevant content of audio) and transcribing. The Who/What/Where/When/Intent frame below is [RECONSTRUCTED]: it is the natural decomposition of a gist summary, not a published agency form.

**Mechanism.** Native speech arrives at 4–6 syllables per second with reduced vowels, merged words and no pauses at the grammar boundaries a textbook shows. A beginner tries to decode every word in order, falls behind by the third word, and gets nothing. Gisting trains the opposite: hold the stream, let most of it pass, and catch the few anchors (names, numbers, places, time words, the verb that carries intent). Once the anchors are reliable, detail fills in around them. Staging the same clip from gist to verbatim turns one minute of audio into fifteen minutes of training and forces the ear to resolve exactly the sounds it was skipping.

**Staged listening ladder.**

| Stage | Passes | Task | Pass line |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Gist | 1 | Write topic + Who + Intent in English in ≤ 20 words | Topic and intent right |
| 2 Detail | 2 | Fill Where, When, numbers, names; one quoted key phrase in the target language | ≥ 4 of 5 fields right |
| 3 Verbatim | 3–5 | Transcribe a 20–30 s segment, then compare to the transcript | ≥ 85% words correct (German), ≥ 80% (Hungarian) |

**Transcription and dictation ladder.** Rung 1: single words from a frequency list (TTS or Forvo) → write. Rung 2: 4–6-word phrases. Rung 3: full sentences at native tempo, two plays. Rung 4: 3-sentence chunks of real audio, three plays. Move up a rung at ≥ 90% letter accuracy on two consecutive sessions; drop a rung after two sessions under 70%. German dictation also trains the B1 writing paper (capitalisation, ß/ss, ie/ei); Hungarian dictation is mostly vowel length and digraphs (gy/ty/ny/sz/zs/cs), which the ear must separate before any suffix can be heard.

**Operational vocabulary selection.** Breadth comes from frequency, not from themed lists. Order: (1) the top 1,000 lemmas of a corpus frequency list — German: the Routledge *A Frequency Dictionary of German* (Jones & Tschirner); Hungarian: the subtitle-derived frequency list on Wiktionary (less clean, but the only free ranked list; strip the proper nouns). (2) Function words and discourse markers first, within the first two weeks. (3) Domain lists tied to purpose — German: Ausbildung/Betrieb/Berufsschule vocabulary, Anmeldung/Aufenthaltstitel/Krankenkasse/Mietvertrag bureaucracy, safety instructions; Hungarian: your own biography and family tree (names of relatives, birthplaces, dates, occupations), the ancestral town and county, documents (anyakönyvi kivonat, útlevél, kérelem), consulate dialogue. Every domain word enters as a chunk in a sentence you will actually say, never bare. Target at B1: ~2,500 lemmas active German, ~2,000 Hungarian.

**ILR/DLPT-style self-assessment.** [DOCUMENTED] The ILR skill-level descriptors and self-assessment can-do statements are public (govtilr.org). Rate yourself monthly, listening and speaking separately: ILR 0+ = isolated words and formulas; 1 = survival needs, simple questions, present tense dominant; 1+ = can handle most survival situations and some limited work needs, past/future with errors; 2 = routine social demands and limited work requirements, connected speech. The app's Wiretap module (Part 2, Module 3) supplies the listening check; a recorded 3-minute monologue graded against the descriptors supplies the speaking check.

**Protocol P-2 — Gisting block.**

1. Material: one 60–120 s clip with transcript (D7). Beginner: slow-news or learner podcast; from month 4: real broadcast.
2. Duration: 15 min per language, 4 days per week.
3. Procedure: Stage 1 blind → score → Stage 2 → score → Stage 3 on one 20–30 s segment → compare to transcript → list every missed word in the burn book under *ear*.
4. Pass: Stage 2 at ≥ 4/5 fields on three consecutive clips at the current rung → raise tempo (slow-news → broadcast → regional/Swiss).

**Protocol P-3 — Dictation ladder.** 5 min at the end of each gisting block, rung as above; score letter accuracy by diff against the transcript; log confusions (ie/ei, ö/ü, a/á, e/é, s/sz) to the burn book.

**Protocol P-4 — Vocabulary intake.** Daily: 10 new lemmas German, 8 Hungarian, each as a chunk in a sentence with a gender-locked article (German) or a possessive/case form (Hungarian), entered into the SRS the same day. Weekly cap 60/50. Retrieval only — no re-reading of lists.

**Protocol P-5 — Monthly self-assessment.** First weekend of each month, per language: 3 Wiretap clips at the next rung up + one recorded 3-minute monologue on a scenario card. Rate against ILR descriptors, record the level in Mission Control. Target line: ILR 1 by month 5 (German) / month 6 (Hungarian); 1+ by month 10 / 12; 2 (German) by month 14.

title: A3. KGB/GRU "legend" training, transferred to language
md:
**What is reported.** [REPORTED] Illegals run by KGB Directorate S (and GRU equivalents) were given a *legend*: a complete fabricated biography, usually anchored on real documents such as the birth certificate of a child who had died young, memorised down to street names, school teachers and childhood illnesses. Training ran for years with native-speaker tutors, often in a third "transit" country so the accent and background acquired there explained any oddities on arrival, and included rehearsed questioning in which trainers attacked the legend from unexpected angles until it held. The best-documented accounts are the Mitrokhin material (Andrew & Mitrokhin), the memoir of the former illegal Jack Barsky, and reporting on the 2010 US arrests, where several agents had lived for years on dead Canadians' identities. Illegals were also expected to think, count and dream in the language. [RECONSTRUCTED] Everything below about *how* that rehearsal was structured, and the transfer to a learner who is telling the truth, is my synthesis. The mythology stops here; the method is what matters.

**Mechanism.** A questioner's pressure attacks retrieval, not knowledge. A pre-built, over-learned narrative with vivid anchors survives because it is retrieved as a chunk rather than assembled word by word. Your legends are true — the apprentice applying for an Ausbildung; the descendant sitting in a consulate interview — which removes the only hard part the illegals had (consistency of a lie) and leaves the useful part: rehearsed fluency about yourself under questioning.

**1. Legend building.** Write each persona as 25–30 facts in the target language: name, age, town, family (each relative: name, relation, birthplace, occupation), work history, why you are here, daily routine, three opinions, three plans. For Hungarian the family-tree facts are the interview itself; get the Hungarian spellings of places and relations right (dédnagyapa = great-grandfather, nagyapa, apa, anya, nővér/húg = older/younger sister). Each fact gets an *anchor memory*: one concrete sensory detail (the smell of the shop floor, the colour of the car) that makes the fact retrievable in the right order.

**2. Cross-examination drill.** A questioner (tutor, exchange partner, or Claude in chat with the legend pasted in) asks 15 questions in random order, in the target language, at natural speed, with follow-up probes (*Warum? Wann genau? Wer noch?* / *Miért? Pontosan mikor? Ki még?*) and one deliberate misunderstanding to force a recovery move. Answers are timed; a pause over 3 s or a switch to English is a fault. Faults go to the burn book as *legend* items and the fact is re-anchored.

**3. Scripted recovery moves.** Over-learn these until they come out before thinking; they buy time and keep the exchange in the target language.

| Move | German | Hungarian |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did not catch it | Wie bitte? / Entschuldigung, das habe ich nicht verstanden. | Tessék? / Elnézést, nem értettem. |
| Ask for repeat | Können Sie das bitte wiederholen? | Megismételné, kérem? |
| Ask for slower | Könnten Sie bitte langsamer sprechen? | Lassabban, kérem. |
| Check meaning | Meinen Sie …? | Úgy érti, hogy …? |
| Buy time | Einen Moment, bitte. / Also … | Egy pillanat. / Hát … |
| Admit limit, keep going | Ich lerne noch Deutsch, aber ich verstehe das Wichtigste. | Még tanulok magyarul, de értem a lényeget. |

**4. In-country and simulated immersion.** The illegals' transit years are not available; the substitutes are persona-locked environments: a German-only desk and a Hungarian-only desk (or two browser profiles and two playlists), phone UI in German, a weekly 30-minute tutor call per language, and a monthly full-day "transit" in one language (menus, podcasts, self-talk, shopping list, journal — all in that language). A planned Europe trip is the real transit: schedule the Hungarian interview rehearsal and the Swiss German exposure around it.

**5. Phonetic mimicry and shadowing.** Shadowing is interpreter training (Lambert) and Arguelles' method, not a KGB invention: play native audio and speak it back with a 0.5–1 s lag, matching pitch, rhythm and reductions, without looking at the text at first. The mimicry target is a specific speaker, not "German": pick one newsreader and one podcast host per language and copy them.

**6. Prosody, discourse markers, fillers, hesitation elimination.** A learner who says *um* is marked as foreign in the first second; one who says *also … genau* or *hát … szóval* is placed as a learner with a good ear. Load the native fillers as reflexes: German *also, na ja, genau, halt, eben, tja, ähm*; Hungarian *hát, szóval, na, ugye, tehát, izé, ööö*. Rule: English never enters the mouth during a session; if the word is missing, use a filler and a paraphrase.

**7. Emotional and sensory encoding.** Stanislavski's sense memory and the keyword mnemonic (Atkinson), relabelled. Every new chunk is learned while performing the action it describes or imagining a scene with a strong sensory anchor; vocabulary that resists gets a keyword image linking the sound to the meaning. This raises retrieval in context, which is where you will need it.

**Protocol P-6 — Legend build.** Week 1 of each language: write the 25–30 facts with anchors in the app (Module 4); record a 2-minute spoken version; re-record weekly until it runs without a pause over 2 s. Pass: 2 minutes, no English, ≤ 2 pauses over 2 s.

**Protocol P-7 — Cross-examination.** Weekly, 15 min per language, from week 3: 15 random questions with probes from a tutor or Claude in chat (paste the legend and the scenario card; ask for natural speed and one deliberate misunderstanding). Score: faults per 15 questions. Pass: ≤ 2 faults twice in a row → move to the next scenario card.

**Protocol P-8 — Shadowing.** Daily 10 min per language: 2 min listen → 3 min shadow blind → 2 min shadow with text → 3 min record one 30 s stretch and compare (A4 self-check). Pass: rhythm and stress matched on the comparison; sound-level errors go to the burn book.

**Protocol P-9 — Fillers and recovery moves.** Drilled as response drills in Module 1 from week 2; one minute of filler-only self-talk at the start of every speaking block. Pass: no English filler in a cross-examination.

**Protocol P-10 — Sensory encoding.** For every chunk that misses twice in the SRS: act it, place it in a scene, or build a keyword image; note the image in the item's explain field.

title: A4. Phonology first
md:
**Mechanism.** [DOCUMENTED] Every FSI Basic Course opens with pronunciation units before grammar because sounds not perceived cannot be stored: a learner who hears *Kirche* and *Kirsche* as the same word stores one wrong entry, and every drill built on it reinforces the error. Minimal pairs train perception; mouth-position cues train production; the record–compare loop closes the gap. Two weeks of daily phonology per language before heavy drilling pays back for the whole year.

**German — the sounds that mark a foreigner.**

| Target | Mouth position | Minimal pairs / drill words |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ich-Laut [ç] (after front vowels and consonants) | Tongue in the *y* of *yes*, blow air over it, no voice | Kirche – Kirsche; Fichte – fischte; Löcher – Löscher; ich, nicht, Milch, Mädchen |
| ach-Laut [x] (after a, o, u, au) | Tongue root toward the soft palate, light friction, no gargle | Nacht – nackt; lachen – lacken; Buch, auch, Koch, Bach |
| ü [yː/ʏ] | Say *ee*, round the lips hard without moving the tongue | Tier – Tür; vier – für; Kissen – küssen; Mutter – Mütter |
| ö [øː/œ] | Say *ay* (no glide), round the lips | lesen – lösen; kennen – können; Hölle – helle |
| r: uvular [ʁ] in onset, vocalised [ɐ] in coda | Onset: light gargle position; coda: an *uh*-coloured vowel, no tongue tip | rot, Rede, Rad vs Bier, Uhr, Lehrer, Mutter |
| Final devoicing | b/d/g/s/v at word end become p/t/k/s/f | Rad = Rat [ʁaːt] but Räder ≠ Räte; Tag [taːk] – Tage; Bund = bunt |
| Glottal onset | Every vowel-initial word or stem starts with a stop; no linking | ein Apfel, ein Auto, beantworten, erinnern, Spiegelei |
| ei vs ie, z, w/v | ei = *eye*, ie = *ee*; z = *ts*; w = *v*, v = *f* in native words | Wein – Wien; Zeit, zu; Wasser, Vater |
| Sentence and word stress | Stress the new/contrastive element; separable prefix stressed, inseparable not; compounds stress the first element | AUFstehen vs verSTEHen; UMfahren (run over) vs umFAHren (drive around); KRANKenhaus |

**Hungarian — the sounds that mark a foreigner.**

| Target | Mouth position | Minimal pairs / drill words |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a [ɒ] vs á [aː] — quality, not just length | a: short, rounded, back, like British *hot*; á: long, open, unrounded, like *father* | kar – kár; hal – hál; sok – sók |
| e [ɛ] vs é [eː] — quality, not just length | e: open like *bet*, slightly lower; é: long *ay* with no glide | szel – szél; kerek – kerék – kérek |
| i/í, o/ó, ö/ő, u/ú, ü/ű — pure length | Same quality, hold the long one twice as long | irt – írt; kor – kór; tör – tőr; örül – őrül; hurok – húrok; ül, tükör vs űr, fű, tűz |
| gy [ɟ], ty [c], ny [ɲ] | Tongue blade flat on the hard palate; one sound, not *d+y* | hagy – had; egy, nagy, magyar; kutya, tyúk; nyár – jár; lány |
| Trilled r | Tongue-tip tap or trill, never American r | rám, vár, kör; long: forr, arra |
| Fixed first-syllable stress | Every word, every time; no English habit of stressing the second syllable | BUdapest, ELnézést, KÖszönöm, DEbrecen |
| Long (double) consonants | Hold the closure; length is phonemic | hal – hall; megy – meggy; szál – száll; ép – épp; tol – toll; kel – kell |
| sz / s / zs / cs | sz = *s*, s = *sh*, zs = *zh* (measure), cs = *ch* | szép, sör, zseb, csak |

**Protocol P-11 — Record–compare–re-record.**

1. Material: 10 pair-words per session from the tables (Forvo or browser TTS for the native model; the app plays TTS where a voice exists).
2. Duration: daily in weeks 1–2, as long as the Sounds block in your plan (5 min in the 45-minute plan, 8 in the 90, 10 in the 150; 15 in Hungarian's sounds-only weeks). After week 2, 5 min, at least 3 days a week; always as the first block.
3. Procedure: play the model twice → say it → record → play model and recording back to back → mark the one feature that differs → fix the mouth position → re-record. Maximum three cycles per word; a word still wrong after three goes to the burn book under *mouth*.
4. Scoring: per word, 1 = match on the target feature by the third cycle, 0 = not.
5. Pass: 9/10 for three sessions on a feature → drop it to weekly maintenance. Perception check at week 2 and monthly: a 20-item minimal-pair listening test (random order, TTS); pass = 18/20.

title: B1. German tactics — pattern drills, not tables [DOCUMENTED drill design; RECONSTRUCTED sequencing]
md:
**1. Cases through signal endings.** The case lives on the determiner, not the noun. Four signal letters carry it: masculine **r/n/m/s** (der, den, dem, des), feminine **e/e/r/r** (die, die, der, der), neuter **s/s/m/s** (das, das, dem, des), plural **e/e/n/r** (die, die, den, der). Two noun-side marks: dative plural adds **-n** (den Männern, den Kindern) and masculine/neuter genitive adds **-(e)s** (des Mannes, des Kindes). Drill the chant once, then never again as a table; from day 3 it is only ever produced inside sentences driven by government:

- Verb government: accusative after sehen, haben, brauchen, kaufen, suchen; dative after helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, antworten. Chain: *Ich helfe dem Chef. (die Kollegin) → Ich helfe der Kollegin. (das Kind) → Ich helfe dem Kind. (die Kollegen) → Ich helfe den Kollegen.*
- Preposition government: dative after aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu; accusative after durch, für, gegen, ohne, um; genitive after wegen, trotz, während. Chain: *Ich fahre mit dem Bus. (der Zug) → Ich fahre mit dem Zug. (das Auto) → Ich fahre mit dem Auto.* / *Wegen des Termins komme ich später. (die Schicht) → Wegen der Schicht komme ich später.*

**2. Gender by cue, and gender-locked chunking.** Learn no noun without its article and plural: *der Tisch, die Tische* — never *Tisch*. Cues that decide most cases: feminine for -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ie, -ik, -ur, -enz and ~90% of nouns in -e (die Lampe, die Maschine); masculine for agent -er, -ling, -ismus, -ist, -or, days, months, seasons, weather (der Montag, der Regen) and most alcoholic drinks (der Wein; das Bier is the exception); neuter for -chen, -lein, -um, -ment, -ma (die Firma is the exception), nouns from infinitives (das Essen), Ge- collectives (das Gebäude, das Gepäck), metals and letters. Chunk drill (response type): cue *Tisch* → *der Tisch, die Tische*; cue *Werkstatt* → *die Werkstatt, die Werkstätten*. Add an adjective in week 3 so the chunk carries an ending: *der große Tisch, die großen Tische*.

**3. Plural patterns** (drill as response, grouped by pattern, then mixed): -e with frequent umlaut on masculine (der Stuhl – die Stühle, der Vertrag – die Verträge); -(e)n on almost all feminines (die Frau – die Frauen, die Maschine – die Maschinen, die Kollegin – die Kolleginnen); -er with umlaut on neuters and some masculines (das Kind – die Kinder, das Haus – die Häuser, der Mann – die Männer); zero (+umlaut) on -er/-el/-en nouns (der Arbeiter – die Arbeiter, der Vater – die Väter, das Mädchen – die Mädchen); -s on loanwords and abbreviations (das Auto – die Autos, der Azubi – die Azubis).

**4. Adjective endings — the three-pattern drill.** One question decides the pattern: does the word before the adjective already show the signal letter?

- Weak (signal already shown by der/die/das/dieser/jeder): adjective takes -e in nominative singular and feminine/neuter accusative, -en everywhere else. *der alte Mann, die alte Frau, das alte Haus, den alten Mann, dem alten Mann, die alten Männer.*
- Strong (no determiner): the adjective carries the signal itself. *guter Wein, gute Milch, gutes Bier, mit gutem Wein, kaltes Wasser* (genitive m/n is the one odd cell: *guten Weines*, because the noun already shows -s).
- Mixed (after ein/kein/mein, which show no signal in nominative masculine and nominative/accusative neuter): the adjective supplies the signal in exactly those three cells, otherwise weak. *ein alter Mann, ein altes Haus, mein neues Werkzeug*; but *eine alte Frau, einen alten Mann, einem alten Mann, meinem neuen Chef.* Drill as substitution chains that swap the determiner and hold the noun: *der neue Vertrag → ein neuer Vertrag → neuer Vertrag → den neuen Vertrag → einen neuen Vertrag.*

**5. Two-way prepositions (wo/wohin).** an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen: motion toward a goal (*wohin?*) → accusative; location (*wo?*) → dative. Drill in verb pairs: legen/liegen, stellen/stehen, setzen/sitzen, hängen. *Ich lege das Werkzeug auf den Tisch. / Das Werkzeug liegt auf dem Tisch.* *Ich gehe in die Werkstatt. / Ich arbeite in der Werkstatt.* *Ich hänge die Jacke an den Haken. / Die Jacke hängt am Haken.*

**6. Separable and inseparable prefix verbs.** Separable (stressed): ab-, an-, auf-, aus-, bei-, ein-, mit-, nach-, vor-, zu-, zurück-, weg-, los-, fest-. Inseparable (unstressed): be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, miss-, ver-, zer-. Dual (um-, über-, unter-, durch-, wieder-) depend on stress and meaning. Four positions to drill for every separable verb: present (*Ich stehe um fünf auf.*), Perfekt with ge- inside (*Ich bin um fünf aufgestanden.*), subordinate clause rejoined (*…, weil ich um fünf aufstehe.*), zu-infinitive (*um fünf aufzustehen*). Inseparable verbs never split and take no ge-: *Ich verstehe das. / Ich habe das verstanden. / …, dass ich das verstehe.*

**7. The sentence bracket (Satzklammer).** Main clause: one element in position 1, finite verb in position 2, everything else in the middle, non-finite part (participle, infinitive, separable prefix) at the end. *Morgen fahre ich mit dem Zug nach Berlin.* Modal cluster: *Ich muss morgen früh aufstehen.* Perfekt: *Ich bin gestern um sechs aufgestanden.* Subordinate clause (weil, dass, ob, wenn, obwohl, damit): conjunction first, finite verb last, after the non-finite part: *…, weil ich morgen früh aufstehen muss. / …, dass er gestern gekommen ist. / …, ob die Schicht um sechs anfängt.* Drill: (a) position-1 swap — *Ich fahre morgen nach Berlin. (Morgen) → Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin.*; (b) main → subordinate transformations with all four conjunctions; (c) tense flip inside a subordinate clause.

**8. TeKaMoLo.** Middle-field order: Temporal → Kausal → Modal → Lokal. *Ich fahre morgen wegen des Termins mit dem Zug nach Berlin.* Drill as expansion: start with *Ich fahre.* and add the four elements in random cue order; the answer must land each in its slot.

**9. Konjunktiv II for politeness.** Six forms carry nearly all B1 politeness: hätte, wäre, könnte, würde, dürfte, möchte. *Ich hätte gern einen Termin. Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen? Wäre es möglich, früher zu kommen? Ich würde gern die Werkstatt sehen. Dürfte ich kurz stören? Ich möchte mich anmelden.* Drill as transformation: blunt → polite.

**10. du/Sie register.** Sie with the Chef/Chefin, every Amt, landlord, doctor, customers, strangers; du with fellow Azubis and once a colleague offers it (*Wir können uns duzen.*). Forms: Sie + infinitive form (*Sie kommen, Sie haben, kommen Sie bitte*), du + -st (*du kommst, du hast, komm bitte*); possessives *Ihr/Ihre* vs *dein/deine*. Drill: du ↔ Sie transformations on workplace requests.

**11. Workplace, apprenticeship, bureaucracy — chunks, not words.** Enter each as a sentence you will say. Ausbildung: *der Ausbildungsvertrag, die Berufsschule, der Betrieb, der Ausbilder / die Ausbilderin, der Azubi, die Frühschicht / Spätschicht, die Werkstatt, die Werkbank, das Werkzeug, die Maschine, die Sicherheitsschuhe, die Schutzbrille, der Feierabend, die Pause, der Urlaub, sich krankmelden, die Krankmeldung, der Lohn / das Gehalt, die Überstunden, die Zeiterfassung.* Bureaucracy: *die Anmeldung beim Einwohnermeldeamt, die Meldebescheinigung, der Aufenthaltstitel, die Ausländerbehörde, das Visum, die Krankenkasse, die Krankenversicherungskarte, die Steuer-ID, das Konto, der Mietvertrag, der Vermieter, die Kaution, die Nebenkosten, der Termin, das Formular ausfüllen, unterschreiben, die Bescheinigung, der Antrag.* Sentence chunks: *Ich möchte mich anmelden. Welche Unterlagen brauche ich? Ich habe einen Termin um zehn. Könnten Sie mir das Formular erklären?*

**12. Swiss German — what differs, when to start.** Swiss Standard German (what is written and what employers expect from a foreigner) differs in small ways: *ss* for *ß*, Helvetisms (*das Velo, das Tram, parkieren, grillieren, der Lehrling*), greetings (*Grüezi, Adieu, Merci*). Spoken Swiss German is Alemannic dialect: *ch* where Standard has *k* (*Chuchichäschtli*), vowels shifted (*Huus* for Haus, *Zyt* for Zeit), no simple past at all, diminutive *-li*, different words for daily things. Goal: listening familiarity only; never try to produce it. Start at month 10 (B1 threshold reached), 10–15 min a week of SRF content (weather and regional news in dialect), rising to 30 min a week in the last quarter; all production stays Hochdeutsch.

title: B2. Hungarian tactics — pattern drills, not tables [DOCUMENTED drill design; RECONSTRUCTED sequencing]
md:
**1. Vowel harmony.** Back vowels: a á o ó u ú. Front unrounded: e é i í. Front rounded: ö ő ü ű. Two-form suffixes (-ban/-ben, -nak/-nek, -val/-vel, -ra/-re, -tól/-től …) pick back vs front. Three-form suffixes (-on/-en/-ön, -hoz/-hez/-höz, -tok/-tek/-tök, -szor/-szer/-ször) pick back / front unrounded / front rounded by the rounding of the last vowel. Mixed stems: i and í are transparent — look past them (papírban, kocsival); é is usually transparent (kávéban); an e in the last syllable usually pulls the word front (Budapesten, októberben); compounds follow their last member (könyvtárban). The deconstructor stores the class per stem, so an unsure stem is looked up, not guessed. Drill: three-stem chains that force both suffix types — *ház / kert / könyv → házban, kertben, könyvben → házon, kerten, könyvön → házhoz, kerthez, könyvhöz.*

**2. Cases as spatial families with a mental map.** Picture a box. Inside it, on top of it, beside it. Each place has three arrows: *being there*, *going there*, *coming from there*. Nine suffixes cover most of daily location talk; the rest are functional.

| Family | Being there | Going there | Coming from there | Back / front / front-rounded chain |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Interior (inside the box) | -ban/-ben | -ba/-be | -ból/-ből | házban, házba, házból · kertben, kertbe, kertből · könyvben, könyvbe, könyvből |
| Surface (on top) | -n / -on/-en/-ön | -ra/-re | -ról/-ről | asztalon, asztalra, asztalról · széken, székre, székről · földön, földre, földről |
| Proximity (beside) | -nál/-nél | -hoz/-hez/-höz | -tól/-től | háznál, házhoz, háztól · kertnél, kerthez, kerttől · könyvnél, könyvhöz, könyvtől |

Functional cases drilled alongside: accusative -t (object), plural -k, dative -nak/-nek (to/for; also marks the possessor: *Péternek a háza*), instrumental -val/-vel (with; v assimilates after a consonant: *házzal, kerttel, busszal, heggyel*; after a vowel *autóval*), terminative -ig (as far as, until), causal-final -ért (for the sake of), essive-formal -ként (as). The count of ~18 varies by analysis; you need these ten actively. Place names use surface or interior by convention: *Budapesten, Pécsen, Magyarországon* but *Debrecenben, Németországban* — learn each city as a chunk with its case.

**3. Suffix stacking order.** Always stem → (linking vowel) → number or possessive → case. *házaimban* = ház + a + i + m + ban (house + link + plural-possessed + my + in). Plural and plural-possessed never co-occur: *házak* (houses) but *házaim* (my houses), never *-k-* with *-i-*. Drill as build chains in the deconstructor: *ház → házak → házakban; ház → házam → házamban; ház → házaim → házaimban.*

**4. Possessive suffixes.** Singular possessed: -m, -d, -a/-e (or -ja/-je), -unk/-ünk (-nk after a vowel), -tok/-tek/-tök, -uk/-ük (-juk/-jük). *házam, házad, háza, házunk, házatok, házuk · kertem, kerted, kertje, kertünk, kertetek, kertjük · autóm, autód, autója, autónk, autótok, autójuk.* Plural possessed inserts -i-: *házaim, házaid, házai, házaink, házaitok, házaik · kertjeim … kertjeik · autóim … autóik.* Whether a stem takes -ja/-je is lexical; the lexicon flags it. Case follows the possessive with final a/e lengthened: *házamban, házában, kertjével, barátaimtól.*

**5. Definite vs indefinite conjugation, and -lak/-lek.** Indefinite: no object, or an indefinite one (*egy könyvet, könyvet, valamit, mindent*). Definite: a definite object (*a könyvet, ezt, azt, őt, Pétert, a házamat*, any possessed noun). Present tense, back stem *olvas* (read): indefinite *olvasok, olvasol, olvas, olvasunk, olvastok, olvasnak*; definite *olvasom, olvasod, olvassa, olvassuk, olvassátok, olvassák*. Front stem *néz* (watch): indefinite *nézek, nézel, néz, nézünk, néztek, néznek*; definite *nézem, nézed, nézi, nézzük, nézitek, nézik*. Non-sibilant stem *lát* (see): indefinite *látok, látsz, lát, látunk, láttok, látnak*; definite *látom, látod, látja, látjuk, látjátok, látják*. Second-person singular indefinite is *-sz* except after s/sz/z, where it is *-ol/-el/-öl*. The *-lak/-lek* ending is first person singular acting on *you*: *Szeretlek. Látlak. Várlak. Kérlek.* Drill: object substitution that flips the conjugation — *Olvasok egy könyvet. (a könyv) → Olvasom a könyvet. (egy újság) → Olvasok egy újságot.*

**6. Coverbs and when they separate.** meg-, el-, ki-, be-, fel-, le-, át-, vissza-, össze-. Attached in a neutral statement: *Megírom a levelet. Elmegyek a boltba. Felkelek hétkor.* Separated and placed after the verb when something else is in focus, after negation, after a question word, and in the imperative: *Nem írom meg. Most írom meg a levelet. Mikor mész el? Menj el! Írd meg!* With a modal or infinitive the coverb stays in front and the verb splits: *El akarok menni. Meg kell írnom.* Drill: neutral → negated, neutral → question-word, neutral → focused element.

**7. Focus-driven word order.** The slot immediately before the verb is the focus. Whatever stands there carries the sentence stress and pushes the coverb behind the verb. Neutral: *Péter holnap elmegy Budapestre.* Focus Péter: *Péter megy el holnap Budapestre.* Focus holnap: *Holnap megy el Péter Budapestre.* Focus Budapestre: *Budapestre megy el Péter holnap.* Question words always sit in focus: *Mikor megy el Péter?* Drill as transformation with the focused element cued.

**8. Linking vowels and stem alternations.** A linking vowel appears before -t, -k and the personal possessives when the stem needs one: *asztalt* (stems in l, r, n, ny, j, ly, s, sz, z, zs take -t directly), *kertet, széket, könyvet* (clusters and most others take one). The linking vowel is o/e/ö by harmony except on *low* stems, which take a/e: *ház → házat, házak, házam; toll → tollat; fal → falat.* Stem types to drill as chunks, each with its accusative, plural and 1SG possessive:

- Shortening stems: *kéz → kezet, kezek, kezem; víz → vizet; tűz → tüzet; út → utat; nyár → nyarat; madár → madarat; levél → levelet; kenyér → kenyeret.* Case suffixes attach to the long form: *kézben, útra, nyáron.*
- v-stems: *ló → lovat, lovak, lovam; kő → követ, kövek; fű → füvet.* Case suffixes attach to the vowel form: *lóra, kőre.*
- Fleeting-vowel stems: *bokor → bokrot; tükör → tükröt; étterem → éttermet; ezer → ezret.*
- Final a/e lengthens before every suffix: *kutya → kutyát, kutyák, kutyám, kutyában; alma → almát.*

**9. Core irregular verbs (present).** *van*: vagyok, vagy, van, vagyunk, vagytok, vannak — and the third person is omitted in a plain predicate (*Ő tanár.* not *Ő tanár van.*). *megy*: megyek, mész, megy, megyünk, mentek, mennek. *jön*: jövök, jössz, jön, jövünk, jöttök, jönnek. *eszik* (indefinite): eszem, eszel, eszik, eszünk, esztek, esznek; definite: eszem, eszed, eszi, esszük, eszitek, eszik. *iszik* (indefinite): iszom, iszol, iszik, iszunk, isztok, isznak; definite: iszom, iszod, issza, isszuk, isszátok, isszák. The -ik verbs take -m in the first person singular in standard and exam Hungarian; you will hear *eszek / iszok* in the street — recognise, do not produce.

**10. Singular after numerals and quantifiers.** The noun and the verb stay singular: *két könyv, három ház, sok ember, néhány barát, hány gyerek? Két ember van itt.* Drill as substitution with the numeral cued.

title: B3. Cross-language bridges, and where each breaks [RECONSTRUCTED]
md:
**Bridge 1 — German separable prefixes ↔ Hungarian coverbs.** Both are verb particles that carry direction or completion and move away from the verb under rules. Rough lexical map: *el-* ≈ weg-/ab- (elmegy ≈ weggehen), *ki-* ≈ aus-/hinaus- (kimegy ≈ hinausgehen), *be-* ≈ ein-/hinein- (bemegy ≈ hineingehen), *fel-* ≈ auf- (felkel ≈ aufstehen), *vissza-* ≈ zurück- (visszajön ≈ zurückkommen), *át-* ≈ hinüber- (átmegy ≈ hinübergehen), *össze-* ≈ zusammen- (összerak ≈ zusammenbauen). Where it breaks: (a) the trigger is different — German separation is syntactic and automatic in every main clause (*Ich stehe auf*), Hungarian separation is information-structural and happens only under focus, negation, question words or imperative (*Felkelek* stays whole in a neutral sentence); (b) *meg-* has no German counterpart at all — it marks completion (*megír* = write to the end), which German leaves to context or adverbs; (c) *le-* only sometimes matches ab-/hinunter- (*leül* = sich hinsetzen, *leír* = aufschreiben). Use the bridge for the idea "particles move", never for word-by-word translation.

**Bridge 2 — German case government ↔ Hungarian case suffixes.** Both languages let the verb or the relation dictate the noun's form, and the spatial logic maps cleanly: in + Dat ≈ -ban/-ben, in + Akk ≈ -ba/-be, aus ≈ -ból/-ből, auf + Dat ≈ -n/-on/-en/-ön, auf + Akk ≈ -ra/-re, von (off) ≈ -ról/-ről, bei ≈ -nál/-nél, zu (toward a person) ≈ -hoz/-hez/-höz, von (away from) ≈ -tól/-től, mit ≈ -val/-vel. The two-way preposition question *wo/wohin* is exactly Hungarian's *being there / going there*; Hungarian just adds the third arrow (*woher*) as its own suffix. Dative experiencers match too: *helfen + Dat* ↔ *segít + -nak/-nek*; *es gefällt mir* ↔ *tetszik nekem*. Where it breaks: German has four cases marked mainly on the article and three genders; Hungarian has ~18 cases marked on the noun and no gender at all. German prepositions are separate words that then demand a case; Hungarian also has postpositions (*mellett, alatt, előtt, mögött, között, után*) that take a bare noun (*a ház mellett*). The German accusative is an article change; the Hungarian accusative is a suffix with a linking vowel and stem alternations. Build Hungarian cases from the spatial map, then note the German preposition as a label, not the reverse.

**Bridge 3 — Austro-Hungarian loanwords.** Centuries of Vienna gave Hungarian a layer of Austrian-German loans that a German learner recognises on sight once the spelling is decoded: *muszáj* (muss sein — must), *sógor* (Schwager), *kuncsaft* (Kundschaft — customer), *cukor* (Zucker), *zsemle* (Semmel), *kifli* (Kipferl), *virsli* (Würstel), *nokedli* (Nockerl), *spenót* (Spinat), *karfiol* (Karfiol), *ribizli* (Ribisel), *krumpli* (Grundbirne, via dialect), *pucol* (putzen), *spórol* (sparen), *smirgli* (Schmirgel — sandpaper), *kuplung* (Kupplung), *stempli* (Stempel), *pult* (Pult — counter), *hokedli* (Hockerl — stool), *sufni* (Schupfen — shed), *suszter* (Schuster), *sláger* (Schlager), *cél* (Ziel), *cérna* (Zwirn), *gróf* (Graf), *herceg* (Herzog), *polgár* (Bürger). The traffic ran both ways: German *Kutsche* (kocsi), *Gulasch*, *Paprika*, *Husar*, *Säbel* (szablya), *Palatschinke* (palacsinta), *Tollpatsch* (talpas), *Dolmetscher* (tolmács). Where it breaks: the sources are Austro-Bavarian dialect forms, so a learner of Hochdeutsch may not know *Kipferl* or *Ribisel*; the loans are spelled phonetically and stressed on the first syllable; many are colloquial or workshop register (fine in a *műhely*, not on a consulate form); meanings drifted (*kuncsaft* is a customer, *sufni* a shed). Treat them as free vocabulary and as a listening aid, never as a grammar bridge.

title: C. Dual-track interference management [RECONSTRUCTED; research on cross-linguistic influence and interleaving]
md:
**Recommendation: a four-week German head start, then both languages at 50/50 under hard separation.** Weeks 1–4 German only (full daily budget). Weeks 5–6 add Hungarian as phonology-only (P-11) while German drills continue. From week 7 the split is 50/50. Reasons: German's sound system and script are the smaller lift from English and stabilise in a month, after which Hungarian's phonology can be built without two unfamiliar systems competing in the same fortnight; the German B1 exam has fixed registration dates and the apprenticeship search needs German first; and with a 61-week budget, anything serial (German to B1, then Hungarian) misses the Hungarian deadline outright.

| Strategy | What it is | Fit for this profile |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Simultaneous from day 1 | Both languages daily, 50/50 | Meets the equal-weight preference; highest interference risk in weeks 1–4 when neither has a stable phonological identity; both first milestones arrive late |
| Staggered start (recommended) | One language gets a 4–6-week head start, then 50/50 | Stable identity for one language before the second competes; small cost to the second language's calendar; interference drops sharply once each has its own sound and script habits |
| German first, Hungarian through German | Reach German B1, then learn Hungarian from German-language materials | Laddering only pays when the base language is B2+; here it delays Hungarian by a year against the same deadline. Reject. Use German-language Hungarian materials later as extra input, not as the route. |

**Separation — four layers, all of them.**

- Time block: the two languages never touch. Weekdays: German in the first slot after the shift (about 3–4:30 PM), Hungarian in the evening (about 7–8:30 PM), with at least two hours between. Weekends: German morning, Hungarian afternoon. Both deadlines are the same; the clock, not the calendar, separates them.
- Place: a different seat or desk per language; a separate browser profile per language with that language's bookmarks, playlists and dictionary; a different notebook colour. Phone UI in German.
- Persona: German = *der Azubi* (Sie-register, workplace, Amt); Hungarian = *a dédunoka* (the great-grandson at the consulate, family register). Switch ritual before every session: 60 seconds of filler-only self-talk in the incoming language (P-9) — *also, genau, na ja …* / *hát, szóval, na …* — until the mouth has changed language.
- Sensory cue: one fixed cue per language held for months — a playlist or ambient sound, a drink, a pen. The cue is an entry key to the right retrieval set, not decoration.

**What interference actually looks like between an Indo-European and a Uralic language.** Grammar transfer is rare because the systems do not overlap: nothing in German prepares a definite conjugation, nothing in Hungarian prepares gender. The real leakage is lexical and prosodic:

- Lexical: German or English words intrude into Hungarian gaps (*… a kertben, aber …*); fillers cross (*also* in Hungarian, *hát* in German); days, numbers and the Austro-Hungarian loans trigger the wrong language (*Zimmer* ≠ *szoba*; *krumpli* ≈ *Kartoffel*).
- Prosodic: German root stress applied to Hungarian (*buDApest* for *BUdapest*); the uvular German r in Hungarian words (Hungarian needs the trill); German final devoicing on Hungarian (*ház* said as *hás*); Hungarian first-syllable stress leaking into German compounds and loan stress.
- Orthographic: *s* (German [z]/[s], Hungarian [ʃ]), *z* (German [ts], Hungarian [z]), *c* (Hungarian [ts]), *v* (Hungarian [v], German [f]) — the same letters, different sounds, and dictation shows it first.
- The two grammatical leaks to watch: German V2 pressure putting the Hungarian verb in second position regardless of focus; Hungarian focus-first order pulling the German finite verb out of position 2.

**Catching it.** Every burn-book entry carries a category; *xfer* is one of them (D9). Weekly error review (D2) replays the week's recordings and the dictation diffs; any item that is right in one language and wrong because of the other is tagged *xfer* and drilled as a contrast pair in the target language (*Haus* vs *ház*: vowel, stress, final consonant). The app's interference guard refuses to open a session in the second language within 90 minutes of closing the first, and shows the persona switch ritual on every session start (Module 5).

**Burnout thresholds and recovery.** Trip-wires: three consecutive days under 50% of planned minutes; drill scores falling for two weeks on sets already passed; skipping the shadowing block because it feels exposing. Recovery: one week on the 45-minute plan; three days of input only (no drills, no recording); one language only for that week — the one with the nearer milestone; then resume at 50/50. Standing rule: one full rest day per week, no language work at all; never let the two languages share the rest day's recovery.

**When to shift the ratio.** 8 weeks before the German B1 exam → 70/30 German. 6 weeks before the consulate interview → 70/30 Hungarian. A language more than 4 weeks behind its milestone line (D5) → 60/40 toward it for 4 weeks, then re-check. During a Europe trip → input-only maintenance for both, Swiss German exposure for German. Never shift below 30% for either language: below that, the quieter one decays faster than the louder one gains.

title: D1. Daily protocol — 45, 90 and 150 minutes
md:
The 45-minute plan is one language's weekday session; the 90-minute plan is one language's weekend session; the 150-minute plan is a single-language day (the German-only weeks 1–4, ratio-shift days, exam run-up). Block order is fixed: phonology while the mouth is fresh → drills while attention is highest → input at lower effort → gisting on a warmed ear → shadowing/legend as performance that uses everything → review to consolidate. Mission Control (Module 5) assembles the blocks and starts the timers.

| Block | Protocol | 45 min | 90 min | 150 min | Log |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Phonology | P-11 | 5 | 8 | 10 | feature, cycles, pass/fail |
| 2 Reflex drills + bridge | P-1 | 12 | 20 | 30 | set, score %, in-time %, misses → burn book |
| 3 Input (reading/listening with text) | A2 vocabulary intake P-4 | 10 | 20 | 35 | source, minutes, new chunks entered |
| 4 Gisting + dictation | P-2, P-3 | 8 | 15 | 20 | clip, stage scores, dictation accuracy |
| 5 Shadowing / legend | P-8; P-6/P-7 on their days | 7 | 15 | 30 | clip, comparison note; legend faults |
| 6 Review | SRS due items, burn book re-drill | 3 | 12 | 15 | due/done, items retired |
| 7 Writing (150 only) | D6 | — | — | 10 | task, error count |

Rules: the timer runs the block, not you; a block ends when the timer ends, with the log line written. No English in the mouth inside a session. Record every shadowing comparison and every legend run — the recordings are the raw material of the weekly error review. Weekday timing: German 3:15–4:15 PM (45-minute plan plus 15 minutes of SRS), Hungarian 7:00–8:00 PM; weekends German 9:00–10:30 AM, Hungarian 2:00–3:30 PM.

title: D2. Weekly protocol
md:
| Day | German | Hungarian | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mon–Thu | 45-min plan + 15 min SRS | 45-min plan + 15 min SRS | Two clock slots, ≥ 2 h apart |
| Fri — assessment and error review | 30-cue mixed drill test, 3 Wiretap clips at current rung, 2-min recorded monologue; then 20-min error review | same | No new material; results go into Mission Control; burn-book items re-tagged and scheduled |
| Sat | 90-min plan + 30-min tutor or Claude cross-examination (P-7) | 90-min plan + 30-min tutor or Claude cross-examination | German morning, Hungarian afternoon |
| Sun | rest | rest | No language work. Non-negotiable. |

Monthly: the first Saturday replaces the normal session with P-5 (3 clips at the next rung up + monologue graded on ILR descriptors) and the 20-item minimal-pair perception test (P-11). Quarterly: a full mock of the external check — German: a timed Goethe B1 model paper (free on the Goethe-Institut site); Hungarian: a 15-minute biography interview with a tutor using only the consulate scenario card.

Error review method (Friday, 20 min per language): replay the week's recordings and dictation diffs at 1.5× speed; every miss gets a burn-book line with a category (D9); the five most repeated lines become next week's "heat set" in the drill engine, scheduled for every session until each passes twice.

title: D3. 12-week onboarding — German (starts week 1; weeks 1–4 at full budget, ~13 h; weeks 5–12 at ~7 h)
md:
Target at week 12: solid A1, first A2 patterns automatic, legend v2 runs 2 minutes clean.

| Weeks | Drill (P-1, P-11) | Read / input (P-4) | Listen / gist / shadow (P-2, P-3, P-8) | Legend / speaking |

title: D5. Milestone map [DOCUMENTED descriptors; RECONSTRUCTED self-tests and dates]
md:
The ILR–CEFR equivalences are approximate (the two scales measure differently); the self-tests are the operational definition this plan uses. A milestone counts only when the self-test passes under its stated conditions, recorded in Mission Control.

| ILR | CEFR | Self-test ("can do X under Y") | German date | Hungarian date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0+ | A1 | Give name, origin, job and family in 10 sentences without notes; answer a slow, repeated question about each; order food and ask a price. Conditions: slow speech, repetition allowed, present tense only. | week 10 (early Jan 2027) | month 5 (late Mar 2027) |
| 1 | A2 | Hold a 10-turn exchange with a landlord, shop or doctor; describe yesterday in the past tense; Stage 1 gist of a slow-news clip 3/3; 2-minute legend monologue with ≤ 3 pauses over 2 s. Conditions: slow-to-normal speech, one repetition. | month 6 (Apr 2027) | month 10 (Aug 2027) |
| 1+ | B1 | 20-turn conversation with a native at natural speed on daily and work topics using only target-language recovery moves; Stage 2 gist at broadcast tempo 4/5; a 100-word workplace message with ≤ 5 errors; read a letter from an office and act on it. Conditions: natural speed, no English, unplanned follow-up questions. | month 11 (Sep 2027); Goethe-Zertifikat B1 or telc B1 sat Nov–Dec 2027 | month 14 (Dec 2027); consulate interview when the application is lodged; optional ECL B1 Hungarian exam as the external check |
| 2 | B2 | Discuss a work problem or an abstract topic at length; follow a native podcast at normal speed with ~80% comprehension; handle an unplanned complication (changed appointment, a dispute) without English. | stretch, end of 2028 | not a target |

**The external check for German.** Goethe-Zertifikat B1 has four modules — Lesen, Hören, Schreiben, Sprechen — each passed separately at 60 of 100 points; telc B1 is the common alternative and is accepted by German authorities for the same purposes. Sprechen Teil 1 is planning something together with a partner, Teil 2 a short presentation, Teil 3 a follow-up discussion — exactly the legend and cross-examination protocols. Register 8–10 weeks ahead; the ratio shift in C applies from registration.

**The external check for Hungarian.** The consulate interview is reported to require a self-sufficient everyday conversation about yourself and your family; the examiner is a consular officer, not a language tester, so biography fluency and recovery moves matter more than grammar range. Treat the tutor-run mock interview (quarterly, D2) as the dress rehearsal.

title: D6. Minimal reading and writing protocol
md:
The B1 exam tests reading and writing as separate modules, so German gets a small, fixed writing dose from week 9; Hungarian writing stays at form-filling and short notes because the interview is spoken.

**Protocol P-12 — German writing, 10 min, three times a week.**

1. Sentence rebuilding (4 min): ten scrambled sentences from the week's drill sets (the app's drill editor can hold them as transformation items); rebuild with correct V2, bracket, subordinate order and TeKaMoLo. Score: sentences fully correct out of ten.
2. One message (6 min) on a Goethe-style prompt, rotating: informal email to a colleague (~80 words: *Hallo Lukas, …*), formal email to an office or landlord (~40 words: *Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, … Mit freundlichen Grüßen*), short opinion post (~80 words).
3. Self-check against a fixed list: noun capitalisation; finite verb in position 2; verb at the end after weil/dass/wenn; case after each preposition; Perfekt participle form and auxiliary; comma before every subordinate clause; ß/ss; du/Sie consistency. Count errors per 100 words; log the categories to the burn book.
4. Pass: ≤ 5 errors per 100 words on three consecutive messages → raise the prompt difficulty (complaint, request for a change, describing a problem at work). Once a month have the tutor or Claude correct one message and compare with your self-check — any error class you missed becomes a burn-book category.

**Protocol P-13 — Hungarian writing, 5 min, twice a week.** Dictation rung as in P-3; copy the legend facts by hand once a week (spelling of names, places, dates: *2005. május 3-án születtem* style date forms); one 30–40-word note (*Kedves Anna! …*) every other week; fill one page of the application form vocabulary (name, birthplace, parents, address). Self-check: vowel length marks, digraphs, suffix harmony.

**Reading.** Inside the daily input block, 10 minutes of reading with the audio when available (graded readers, Nachrichtenleicht, FSI basic sentences; Hungarian: FSI texts, HungarianPod101 transcripts, then simple news). From month 6, German reading switches to authentic bureaucracy: an Anmeldung form, a sample Mietvertrag, a Krankenkasse letter, an Ausbildungsvertrag — read, extract the action required, write the reply. That is the B1 Lesen module and the real-world task in one.

title: D9. Error log — the burn book [RECONSTRUCTED; error-logging practice from DLI-style transcription review]
md:
**Capture.** One line per error, written the moment it is found (drill miss, dictation diff, shadowing comparison, legend fault, tutor correction): date · language · what you produced · the correct form · category · source block. The app writes drill misses automatically; everything else you type in the Mission Control error log in under ten seconds.

**Categories (one per line, exactly these):** *mouth* (pronunciation), *ear* (misheard or not heard), *case* (German case / Hungarian case suffix), *gender* (German article), *adj* (adjective ending), *order* (V2, bracket, subordinate; Hungarian focus), *conj* (definite/indefinite, person endings), *coverb* (position), *prefix* (German separable/inseparable), *harmony* (wrong suffix vowel), *stem* (linking vowel, alternation), *lex* (wrong word or missing word), *xfer* (interference from the other language or English), *legend* (biography fault or pause), *spell* (writing).

**Drill out.**

1. Every burn-book line becomes a drill item: cue = the sentence with the slot blanked, answer = the correct form, explain = what you produced and why it was wrong. The app does this on "Add to drills".
2. New error items enter the SRS at a 1-day interval regardless of the family's normal schedule; three consecutive passes at least 7 days apart retire the line.
3. Friday: the five most repeated lines of the week form the heat set, which opens every session the following week.
4. Monthly: the category histogram decides the next month's extra block — the category with the most open lines gets 5 added minutes in every session until it drops out of first place.
5. *xfer* lines are drilled as contrast pairs in the language that lost (Haus/ház, s/sz), never by translating.

**Pass line for the book itself.** Fewer than 15 open lines per language, none older than 30 days. More than 40 open lines means intake is outrunning consolidation: cut P-4 vocabulary intake by half for two weeks.
